implementation_notes: Kotlin expresses fork/join with coroutines: inside coroutineScope, async { } forks a child task and the scope's exit joins it; awaitAll (or awaiting each Deferred) collects the results. Dispatchers.Default runs the coroutines on a shared work-stealing thread pool on the JVM (and a multi-threaded pool on Kotlin/Native), so the classic per-worker deques and pool are runtime property, not user code. Structured concurrency makes failure and cancellation part of the join - a failing child cancels the scope instead of leaking a task - which is stronger than the classic task model. Reach for the raw JVM ForkJoinPool/RecursiveTask only to interoperate with existing Java code or to tune pool metrics.
pitfalls: async inherits the caller's dispatcher: forked from Dispatchers.Main the children run on the main thread and there is no parallelism - put withContext(Dispatchers.Default) (or IO) around the fork.
A child failure cancels the whole coroutineScope: fire-and-forget work needs its own scope or supervisor, not async in the same scope.
awaitAll fails fast on the first exception while siblings keep running until cancellation propagates - catch per task if partial results matter.
